rv.q: It perfectly distils the comic tone and is a rare blast of sunshine at the National.
It is all, in its irrepressible, rambunctious way, every bit as clever as it is deliciously daft.
This knowing mix of satire, filth, clowning, pastiche, wartime derring-do and romance absolutely hit my sweet spot.
So it’s even more of a pleasure to report that this venture — anchored by Caroline Quentin as an adorable, potty-mouthed Mrs Malaprop — is a joyous romp.
When it doubles down on being a silly, rollicking, escapist comedy, it’s the giddiest night of theatre you’ll have all summer.
It’s always relatively entertaining, often very funny indeed, but its frothiness becomes tiresome after a while and it’s more celebratory than interrogative of the time it’s portraying.

The script has a self-consciously Boy's Own 'whizzo' feel and drips with arch knowingness and nods to its own theatricality, which is amusing enough but prevents us from caring much about what happens to anyone.
It doesn’t quite work, because it’s easier to laugh than to cry over these thinly drawn characters.
It’s relentlessly chucklesome, but almost aggressively lacking in wider purpose.
The silliness and humour sometimes sparks but Sheridan’s razor sharp lines and social class critiques become mostly toothless in this transposition.
It’s a brilliant start to a night of comedy gold.
All of this, not to mention composer Paul Englishby’s roof-raising company jitterbug number, is immaculately meshed in director Emily Burns’ perfectly paced, ideally calibrated production.
The fun never stops and at times you miss punchlines as you’re still laughing at the previous joke.
"Jack Again" proves the perfect tonic to the miserable few years we have been through.

Mark Thompson’s design illustrates the production’s sweet spot: a technicolour combination of comic book and live action, Englishness as an aesthetic and a myth. 'Jack Absolute' is more content to cuddle up to that myth than to seriously challenge it, but as pure summer fizz, it goes down a treat.
The result is a play which frequently, rightly, brings the house down.
With a skilled and hugely likeable cast, it’s genuinely funny and charming, spectacularly, beautifully staged, and ultimately quite moving.
An enthusiastic first night reception suggests that it achieves that, thanks to some extrovert comedy acting and especially thanks to the pairing of Caroline Quentin and Peter Forbes.
The writing duo undoubtedly have created another rollickingly good farce.
Jack Again is hilarious; proper laugh out loud, trying to suppress a snort kind of laughter.

cn.t: Bean and Chris's WWII-set update of Sheridan's "The Rivals" earns mostly positive reviews as a crowd-pleasing, irreverent farce, though critics note it doesn't quite match "One Man, Two Guvnors" and favors relentless gags over emotional depth.
